name: Computer Networks: Core Concepts & Disambiguation
details:
Computer Networks: Comprehensive Conceptual Knowledge & Disambiguation Engine

This interactive knowledge map is organized not merely by lecture sequence, but by foundational network abstractions, protocol mechanisms, and rigorous technical disambiguations.

Core Focus: Disambiguating subtle, often-confused networking concepts (Flow vs Congestion Control, GBN vs SR, Tahoe vs Reno vs NewReno, HTTP/1 vs 2 vs 3, Transport vs Network Layer, Karn's Ambiguity, TLS 1.2 vs 1.3).
  • Scope: Application Layer Systems, Transport Layer Primitives, RDT State Machines, TCP/UDP Architectures, Congestion/Flow Engineering, and Cryptographic Security.
  • Source Base: Sadi Sir's Lectures (Part 1), Kurose & Ross (8th ed.), Forouzan (5th ed.), and authoritative RFC specifications (RFC 768, 793, 1122, 2018, 5681, 6298, 8446).

children.name: 1. Application Layer Systems & Web Architectures
children.details:
Application Layer Architecture & Protocols

The Application Layer contains user-facing programs and network services communicating across the Internet. Unlike lower layers implemented in the OS kernel or network hardware, application protocols run entirely in user space.

Primary Function: Defines message formats, syntax, semantics, and exchange sequences between user processes.

children.name: 1.1 Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer (P2P)
children.details:
Architecture Disambiguation: Client-Server vs P2P

Metric Client-Server Peer-to-Peer (P2P)
Host Role Dedicated, always-on server; transient clients. Arbitrary end-systems act as both client and server (servents).
Addressing Fixed, well-known IP address. Dynamic, churn-heavy residential IP addresses.
Scalability Server bandwidth bottlenecks as $N$ clients grow: $T \ge \max(NF/u_s, F/d_{\min})$. Self-Scalability: Peers bring service capacity as well as demand: $T \ge \max(F/u_s, F/d_{\min}, NF / (u_s + \sum u_i))$.
Management Centralized, highly controlled. Decentralized, complex NAT traversal and peer churn.

children.name: Client-Server: Centralized Bottleneck
children.details: Server upload capacity $u_s$ must support $N$ clients. Time to distribute a file of size $F$ scales linearly with $N$: $D_{cs} \ge NF / u_s$.

children.name: P2P: Self-Scalability & Churn
children.details: Each peer that downloads also uploads chunks to other peers. Total upload capacity grows linearly with $N$ ($u_s + \sum u_i$), keeping distribution time bounded.

children.name: 1.2 Web & HTTP Evolution (1.0 vs 1.1 vs 2 vs 3)
children.details:
Evolution of Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)

Version Transport Connection Model Head-of-Line (HOL) Blocking
HTTP/1.0 TCP Non-persistent: 1 TCP connection per object (2 RTT + transfer). High (serial connection overhead).
HTTP/1.1 TCP Persistent connection (reused for multiple objects). Optional pipelining. Application-level HOL blocking: If object 1 is delayed, objects 2, 3 must wait in line.
HTTP/2 TCP Binary framing layer. Interleaved multiplexed streams over 1 TCP connection. Server Push. HPACK header compression. TCP-level HOL blocking: A single lost TCP packet halts all multiplexed streams in that connection!
HTTP/3 QUIC (UDP) Independent streams at transport layer. 0-RTT/1-RTT connection setup combining transport + TLS 1.3 handshake. Connection migration via 64-bit Connection ID. Zero HOL Blocking: Packet loss on stream A does not stall stream B.

children.name: HTTP/1.0: Non-Persistent (2 RTT/Object)
children.details: Opens a new TCP connection for every single inline asset (images, CSS). Wastes RTT and server memory.

children.name: HTTP/1.1: Persistent & App-Level HOL
children.details: Reuses open TCP connection. Pipelining was rarely deployed due to middlebox bugs and FIFO response requirements.

children.name: HTTP/2: Binary Framing & TCP HOL
children.details: Splits messages into binary frames (HEADERS, DATA) tagged with Stream IDs. Eliminates app HOL, but single TCP loss halts all streams.

children.name: HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP (Zero HOL)
children.details: Runs over UDP. Streams are independent at the transport layer. Lost packets only stall their own stream.

children.name: 1.3 Web State: Cookies & Caching
children.details:
State Management & Performance Optimization

  • Cookies (State over Stateless HTTP): HTTP is stateless. Cookies restore state via 4 components:
    1. Set-Cookie: key=val header in HTTP server response.
    2. Cookie: key=val header in subsequent client requests.
    3. Cookie file kept on client host and managed by user browser.
    4. Backend database at web site mapping cookie IDs to user session, shopping cart, or authentication credentials.
  • Web Caching (Proxy Servers): Satisfies client requests without involving the origin server. Reduces response time and access link traffic.
  • Conditional GET (Cache Validation):
    • Client/Proxy cache sends: If-Modified-Since: <date> or If-None-Match: <etag>.
    • If not modified: Server returns HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified with empty entity body, saving link bandwidth.
    • If modified: Server returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK with fresh data payload.

children.name: Cookies: 4-Component Architecture
children.details: Set-Cookie header -> Client storage -> Cookie header in future requests -> Server database mapping.

children.name: Conditional GET: 304 Not Modified
children.details: Uses If-Modified-Since or ETag headers to validate freshness without transferring payload.

children.name: 1.4 DNS: Iterative vs Recursive Resolution
children.details:
Disambiguation: Iterative vs Recursive DNS Resolution

Feature Iterative Query Recursive Query
Server Action Queried server replies: "I don't know the answer, but ask this next server." (returns referral). Queried server replies: "I will find the answer for you." (assumes full burden).
Workload Location Workload stays on the Local DNS Server (resolver). Workload cascades upward through Root and TLD servers.
Internet Standard Standard across Root and TLD servers to prevent central overload. Used only between residential host and Local DNS Server.

DNS Record Types: A (Host->IPv4), AAAA (Host->IPv6), NS (Domain->Authoritative Server), CNAME (Alias->Canonical Name), MX (Domain->Mail Server).

children.name: Iterative Query (Referral Chains)
children.details: Queried name server returns the IP address of the next hierarchical server to contact.

children.name: Recursive Query (Delegated Burden)
children.details: The queried server contacts the next server on the client's behalf and returns the final answer.

children.name: DNS Record Types: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, MX
children.details: A=IPv4, AAAA=IPv6, NS=Authoritative Server, CNAME=Canonical Alias, MX=Mail Server.

children.name: 1.5 Email Architecture: Push vs Pull Protocols
children.details:
Disambiguation: Push Protocol (SMTP) vs Pull Protocols (POP3/IMAP)

  • SMTP (Push): Used by sending client to deposit mail at sender's mail server, and between mail servers over TCP port 25. Operates on 7-bit ASCII (MIME encodes binary attachments).
  • POP3 (Pull): Connects to mail server to retrieve messages. Typically download-and-delete. Stateless across sessions.
  • IMAP (Pull): Connects to mail server to manage messages in server folders. Stateful across sessions. Allows partial download of headers and attachments.
  • Webmail (HTTP/HTTPS): Browser uses HTTP to view and compose mail; the mail server still uses SMTP to deliver messages to destination mail servers.

children.name: SMTP (Push Protocol, Port 25)
children.details: Pushes mail from client to sender server, and server-to-server. Requires 7-bit ASCII.

children.name: POP3 vs IMAP (Pull Protocols)
children.details: POP3 downloads and is stateless; IMAP preserves folder hierarchy and is stateful across sessions.

children.name: 2. Transport Layer Foundations & Demultiplexing
children.details:
Transport Layer Principles

Provides logical end-to-end communication between application processes on different hosts.

Fundamental Problem: How to take packets delivered host-to-host by IP and route them to the exact executing process socket.

children.name: 2.1 Transport Layer vs Network Layer
children.details:
Disambiguation: Transport Layer vs Network Layer

Dimension Transport Layer (L4) Network Layer (L3)
Communication Scope Process-to-Process (Socket-to-Socket) Host-to-Host (Machine-to-Machine)
Addressing Port Numbers (16-bit, 0–65535) IP Addresses (32-bit IPv4 / 128-bit IPv6)
Implementation Location Strictly at End-Systems (Hosts) in the OS Kernel. Network core routers ignore L4 headers. Across Every Host and Core Router in the Internet.
Service Capabilities Can enhance underlying service: converts unreliable IP into reliable, in-order byte stream (TCP). Best-effort datagram delivery. Packets can be lost, reordered, corrupted, or duplicated.

children.name: Process-to-Process vs Host-to-Host
children.details: Transport communicates between specific OS process sockets; Network communicates between physical network interfaces.

children.name: End-to-End Principle
children.details: Intelligence and state are maintained solely at the end hosts; the network core routers remain simple packet forwarders.

children.name: 2.2 Multiplexing & Demux: 2-Tuple vs 4-Tuple
children.details:
Disambiguation: UDP 2-Tuple Demux vs TCP 4-Tuple Demux

Protocol Demultiplexing Key Socket Mapping Behavior
UDP (Connectionless) 2-Tuple: (Dest IP, Dest Port) Two UDP packets arriving from different source IPs or source ports with the same destination port are delivered to the exact same socket.
TCP (Connection-Oriented) 4-Tuple: (Src IP, Src Port, Dest IP, Dest Port) Each unique client connection is directed to a separate dedicated socket spawned by the server (accept loop), even though all initial handshakes arrive at port 80/443.

Port Number Space (16 bits): Well-Known (0–1023), Registered (1024–49151), Ephemeral/Private (49152–65535).

children.name: UDP 2-Tuple: (Dest IP, Dest Port)
children.details: Shared socket for all senders targeting the destination port. Source IP/port are read inside the message payload.

children.name: TCP 4-Tuple: (Src IP, Src Port, Dest IP, Dest Port)
children.details: Unique dedicated socket per active connection. Server accept() forks or binds a separate socket structure.

children.name: Port Classification (16-bit space)
children.details: Well-known (0-1023), Registered (1024-49151), Dynamic/Ephemeral (49152-65535).

children.name: 3. Reliable Data Transfer (RDT) Theory & Pipelining
children.details:
Reliable Data Transfer (RDT) State Machines

RDT models the progressive construction of reliability over channels that exhibit bit corruption, duplicate packet delivery, packet reordering, and complete packet loss.

children.name: 3.1 RDT Protocol Evolution (1.0 -> 3.0)
children.details:
Step-by-Step RDT State Machine Progression

  • rdt 1.0: Completely reliable underlying channel. No bit errors, no losses. Trivial sender/receiver state machines.
  • rdt 2.0: Channel with bit corruption. Introduces Checksum, ACK (positive feedback), and NAK (negative feedback).
    Fatal Flaw: If the ACK/NAK packet itself gets corrupted, sender cannot know what receiver said!
  • rdt 2.1: Solves corrupted feedback by introducing a 1-bit Sequence Number (0 and 1) in data packets. If ACK/NAK is corrupted, sender retransmits. Receiver detects duplicate sequence number, discards duplicate data, and re-ACKs.
  • rdt 2.2: NAK-Free Protocol. Replaces NAKs with duplicate ACKs. Receiver ACKs the last correctly received packet sequence number. An ACK for the previous packet serves as an implicit NAK for the current packet.
  • rdt 3.0: Channel with bit errors AND packet loss. Introduces a Countdown Timer. Sender retransmits packet on timer expiration. Handles packet loss, lost ACKs, and premature timeouts.

children.name: rdt 1.0: Flawless Channel
children.details: Assumes underlying channel has zero packet loss and zero bit corruption. No ACKs, no timers.

children.name: rdt 2.0: Checksum & Fatal Feedback Flaw
children.details: Introduces Checksums and ACK/NAK. Fatal flaw: sender cannot interpret a corrupted ACK/NAK packet.

children.name: rdt 2.1: 1-Bit Sequence Number
children.details: Adds 1-bit sequence number (0 or 1). Sender retransmits on corrupted ACK; receiver discards duplicates.

children.name: rdt 2.2: NAK-Free Protocol
children.details: Eliminates NAKs entirely by sending duplicate ACKs for the last good packet.

children.name: rdt 3.0: Countdown Timer for Packet Loss
children.details: Adds countdown retransmission timer to recover from dropped packets, dropped ACKs, and network delay.

children.name: 3.2 Stop-and-Wait vs Pipelined Protocols
children.details:
Disambiguation: Stop-and-Wait vs Pipelined Utilization

Stop-and-Wait Efficiency Formula:

$$U_{\text{sender}} = \frac{L/R}{\text{RTT} + L/R}$$

Example: 1 Gbps link ($R = 10^9\text{ bps}$), 30 ms RTT ($0.03\text{ s}$), 1 KB packet ($L = 8000\text{ bits}$).

Transmission delay $t_{\text{trans}} = 8000 / 10^9 = 8\,\mu\text{s}$.

$$U_{\text{sender}} = \frac{0.000008}{0.03 + 0.000008} \approx 0.00027 \quad (0.027\%!)$$

The link is idle 99.97% of the time! Pipelining solves this by allowing $N$ in-flight packets:

$$U_{\text{pipelined}} = \frac{N \times (L/R)}{\text{RTT} + L/R}$$

Choosing $N = \lceil (\text{RTT} \times R) / L \rceil$ yields 100% link utilization.

children.name: Stop-and-Wait: <0.1% Link Utilization
children.details: Sender must wait a full RTT for ACK before sending next segment, leaving link idle 99.9% of the time.

children.name: Pipelined Utilization: N * (L/R) / RTT
children.details: Keeps the pipeline full with N in-flight unacknowledged packets. 100% utilization when N >= Bandwidth-Delay Product.

children.name: 3.3 Go-Back-N (GBN) vs Selective Repeat (SR)
children.details:
Deep Disambiguation: Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat

Dimension Go-Back-N (GBN) Selective Repeat (SR)
Acknowledgment Type Cumulative ACK: ACK(n) acknowledges all packets up to and including $n$. Individual ACK: ACK(n) acknowledges only packet $n$.
Sender Timers Single timer for the oldest unacknowledged packet (base). Independent timer for each unacknowledged packet.
Receiver Buffering No buffering. Out-of-order packets are discarded immediately. Re-ACKs highest in-order packet. Buffers out-of-order packets until missing gaps are filled, then delivers batch to application.
Retransmission Cost Retransmits ALL $N$ packets in window on timeout (wasteful over lossy links). Retransmits only the specific lost packet.
Window Size Constraint $N \le 2^k - 1$ $N \le 2^{k-1}$ (Window size cannot exceed half sequence space to prevent ambiguity between old duplicates and new packets).

children.name: GBN: Cumulative ACK & 1 Timer
children.details: Receiver discards all out-of-order packets. Single timer for base. Retransmits entire window on timeout.

children.name: SR: Individual ACKs & Buffer
children.details: Receiver buffers out-of-order packets. Per-packet timers. Retransmits only lost packets.

children.name: Window Size Rule: N <= 2^(k-1)
children.details: In SR, window size cannot exceed half the sequence space to avoid ambiguity between old and new packets.

children.name: 4. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Architecture
children.details:
TCP Architecture & Protocol State Machines (RFC 793, 1122, 5681)

TCP provides connection-oriented, full-duplex, reliable byte-stream delivery with end-to-end flow control and network-wide congestion control.

children.name: 4.1 TCP Header Layout & Semantics (20-60 Bytes)
children.details:
TCP Header Structure & Field Semantics (Slide 216 Diagram)

  • Source & Destination Ports (16 bits each): Process demultiplexing endpoints.
  • Sequence Number (32 bits): The byte-stream index of the first data byte in this segment. Under ISN (Initial Sequence Number), randomly generated to prevent cross-connection collision.
  • Acknowledgment Number (32 bits): The next byte number the receiver expects to receive. Cumulative in TCP.
  • HLEN (4 bits): Number of 32-bit words in header (minimum 5 = 20 bytes, maximum 15 = 60 bytes).
  • Flags (6 bits):
    • URG: Urgent pointer valid.
    • ACK: Acknowledgment field valid (set in all segments after initial SYN).
    • PSH: Receiver should push data to app immediately without waiting for buffer to fill.
    • RST: Abruptly reset/refuse the connection.
    • SYN: Synchronize sequence numbers during connection establishment.
    • FIN: Sender has finished transmitting data (closes one direction of full-duplex stream).
  • Window Size (16 bits): Advertised receive window (rwnd) in bytes for flow control. Multiplied by Window Scale Option (RFC 7323) up to $2^{30}$ bytes.
  • Checksum (16 bits): 1's complement sum over header, data, and 12-byte IP pseudo-header (Source IP, Dest IP, Protocol 6, TCP Length).
  • Options (0 – 40 bytes): MSS (Maximum Segment Size), SACK (Selective Acknowledgment), Timestamps.

children.name: 6 Control Flags (URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN)
children.details: SYN starts, FIN cleanly ends, RST abruptly resets, ACK confirms bytes, PSH bypasses buffer, URG points to urgent data.

children.name: Sequence & Ack Numbers (Byte Stream)
children.details: Counts bytes, not packets. ACK indicates the next expected byte.

children.name: Window Size & Options (MSS, SACK, Scale)
children.details: 16-bit rwnd for flow control. Window scale option shifts up to 1GB. SACK reports received non-contiguous blocks.

children.name: 4.2 Three-Way Handshake & SYN Floods
children.details:
Connection Establishment & Attack Vector Disambiguation

Three-Way Handshake:

  1. Client -> Server: SYN=1, seq=client_isn (No data payload).
  2. Server -> Client: SYN=1, ACK=1, seq=server_isn, ack=client_isn + 1. Server allocates TCB (Transmission Control Block) and buffers.
  3. Client -> Server: ACK=1, seq=client_isn + 1, ack=server_isn + 1. May carry first application data bytes!

SYN Flood Attack vs SYN Cookies Defense:

  • SYN Flood: Attacker transmits flood of SYNs with spoofed source IPs and never completes Step 3. Server connection queue fills with half-open connections, refusing legitimate users.
  • SYN Cookies (Defense): Server allocates zero memory on receiving SYN. It crafts server_isn using a cryptographic hash: $$server\_isn = \text{Hash}(src\_ip, src\_port, dst\_ip, dst\_port, \text{secret}) + \text{timestamp}$$ When legitimate client sends ACK with ack = server_isn + 1, server verifies hash and only then allocates socket memory!

children.name: 3-Way Handshake Sequence
children.details: Client SYN -> Server SYN-ACK (allocates state) -> Client ACK (completes connection).

children.name: SYN Flood Attack
children.details: Spoofed SYNs overwhelm server's half-open connection table, denying service to legitimate clients.

children.name: SYN Cookies Defense
children.details: Server allocates zero state upon SYN, encoding state into ISN hash; verifies upon final ACK.

children.name: 4.3 Connection Teardown & TIME_WAIT (2MSL)
children.details:
Connection Teardown & Why TIME_WAIT is Essential

TCP is full-duplex, so each direction must be closed independently:

  1. Client sends FIN=1, seq=u -> Enters FIN_WAIT_1.
  2. Server sends ACK=1, ack=u+1 -> Client enters FIN_WAIT_2. Server enters CLOSE_WAIT (server can still send remaining data).
  3. Server finishes data, sends FIN=1, seq=w -> Server enters LAST_ACK.
  4. Client sends ACK=1, ack=w+1 -> Client enters TIME_WAIT for $2 \times \text{MSL}$. Server receives ACK and enters CLOSED.

Why is TIME_WAIT Necessary? (Two Reasons):

  • Reason 1 (Reliable Termination): If Client's final ACK is lost, Server retransmits FIN. If Client had already closed immediately, it would respond with RST, causing an error on Server rather than a clean close.
  • Reason 2 (Old Packet Drain): Prevents old wandering duplicate segments from a prior connection incarnation from being mistakenly delivered to a new connection reusing the same 4-tuple. MSL is Maximum Segment Lifetime (typically 30–60s; $2\text{MSL} = 1\text{–}2\text{ min}$).

children.name: 4-Way FIN/ACK Teardown
children.details: Each direction closes independently. FIN -> ACK -> FIN -> ACK.

children.name: TIME_WAIT State & 2MSL Quarantine
children.details: Client waits 2MSL (60-120s) to re-ACK if final ACK was lost, and to flush old duplicate packets from network.

children.name: 5. Flow Control & Buffer Management
children.details:
Flow Control Architecture

Definition: An end-to-end speed matching mechanism that prevents a fast sender from overflowing the receiver's application buffer.

Governing Equation: $\text{rwnd} = \text{RcvBuffer} - [\text{LastByteRcvd} - \text{LastByteRead}]$.

children.name: 5.1 Sliding Window Dynamics & Zero-Window Probes
children.details:
Sliding Window Transitions (Slide 250 Diagram)

  • Closing Window: Left edge advances right as bytes are sent and acknowledged.
  • Opening Window: Right edge advances right as receiver application reads data from buffer, expanding rwnd.
  • Shrinking Window: Right edge moves left (strongly discouraged by RFC 1122).
  • Zero-Window Deadlock Problem: If receiver advertises rwnd = 0, sender stops transmitting. Later, receiver's app reads data and receiver sends an ACK with rwnd > 0. If this ACK is lost, both sides wait forever (Deadlock)!
  • Persistence Timer Solution: When rwnd = 0, sender starts a Persistence Timer. On expiry, sender sends a 1-byte Probe Segment. The receiver must ACK this probe, re-advertising the current rwnd and breaking the deadlock.

children.name: Sliding Window Edges (Open, Close, Shrink)
children.details: Left edge closes on ACKs; right edge opens as receiver application reads data.

children.name: Zero-Window Probes & Persistence Timer
children.details: 1-byte probe segment sent periodically when rwnd=0 to prevent deadlock from lost window update ACKs.

children.name: 5.2 Silly Window Syndrome: Nagle vs Clark
children.details:
Disambiguation: Sender-Side vs Receiver-Side Silly Window Syndrome

The Pathology: Tiny packets (e.g. 1-byte data + 40-byte TCP/IP header = 41-byte packet with 2.4% efficiency!) flood the network.

Entity Problem Cause RFC Solution
Sender Side Application generates data 1 byte at a time (e.g. Telnet keystrokes) and immediately transmits. Nagle's Algorithm (RFC 896): If data $\ge \text{MSS}$, send immediately. Otherwise, send only if all previous packets have been acknowledged. While waiting for ACK, buffer incoming bytes.
Receiver Side Application reads data 1 byte at a time from full buffer, immediately advertising rwnd = 1 to sender. Clark's Solution (RFC 813): Do not advertise a window update until the receiver buffer has space for at least $\min(\text{MSS}, \text{Buffer}/2)$. Otherwise, keep advertising rwnd = 0.

children.name: Nagle's Algorithm (Sender-Side Solution)
children.details: Buffers tiny writes until full MSS is assembled OR previous packet ACK has arrived.

children.name: Clark's Solution (Receiver-Side Solution)
children.details: Advertises rwnd=0 until buffer can accommodate at least min(MSS, Buffer/2).

children.name: 6. Congestion Control & Algorithmic Regimes
children.details:
TCP Congestion Control Engineering

Prevents sender from injecting more traffic than intermediate network routers can handle. Governed by $W = \min(\text{cwnd}, \text{rwnd})$.

children.name: 6.1 Flow Control vs Congestion Control Disambiguation
children.details:
Core Disambiguation: Flow Control vs Congestion Control

Metric Flow Control Congestion Control
Objective Protect the Receiver's application buffer from overflow. Protect the Subnet routers & links from packet drops.
Controlling Variable rwnd (Receiver Window, advertised explicitly in TCP header). cwnd (Congestion Window, maintained locally by sender).
Feedback Mechanism Direct, explicit (Receiver writes window value in header). Implicit (packet loss, timeouts, duplicate ACKs) or explicit (ECN).

children.name: Receiver Buffer vs Router Buffer
children.details: Flow control protects the destination host buffer; congestion control protects shared intermediate routers.

children.name: rwnd vs cwnd Interaction
children.details: Effective transmission window W = min(cwnd, rwnd). Minimum bottleneck constraint always wins.

children.name: 6.2 AIMD: Additive Increase / Multiplicative Decrease
children.details:
AIMD: Stability & Fairness Proof

  • Additive Increase: Probing for spare capacity. Increase cwnd by 1 MSS per RTT: $$\text{cwnd} = \text{cwnd} + \frac{\text{MSS} \times \text{MSS}}{\text{cwnd}} \quad \text{on each ACK}$$
  • Multiplicative Decrease: Reacting to congestion. Cut cwnd in half on packet drop: $$\text{cwnd} = \text{cwnd} / 2$$
  • Why AIMD? (Chiu & Jain Vector Space Proof): AIMD drives competing flows along the efficiency line toward the 45-degree Equal Share (Fairness) line. AI shifts parallel to fairness line; MD points directly toward the origin, converging to fairness!

children.name: Additive Increase (+1 MSS / RTT)
children.details: Increases cwnd linearly to probe bandwidth without causing sudden packet drops.

children.name: Multiplicative Decrease (Halve cwnd)
children.details: Cuts rate immediately by 50% to rapidly drain overwhelmed router queues.

children.name: Chiu-Jain Fairness Convergence
children.details: Proves vector trajectory converges to optimal bandwidth allocation and fairness across flows.

children.name: 6.3 Congestion Phases: Slow Start vs Avoidance
children.details:
Congestion Phases & Fast Retransmit (Slide 270 Diagram)

  • Slow Start: Initial phase. cwnd = 1 MSS. Doubles every RTT ($1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8 \dots$). Increases by 1 MSS on every incoming ACK. Continues until cwnd >= ssthresh.
  • Congestion Avoidance: Linear growth (+1 MSS per RTT). Begins when cwnd >= ssthresh.
  • Fast Retransmit: Upon receiving 3 Duplicate ACKs (4 identical ACKs total), sender infers packet loss immediately without waiting for timer expiration, and retransmits missing segment.

children.name: Slow Start (Exponential cwnd Doubling)
children.details: Doubles cwnd every RTT to quickly ramp up transmission to pipe capacity.

children.name: Congestion Avoidance (Linear AIMD)
children.details: Increases cwnd by 1 MSS per RTT once ssthresh is crossed.

children.name: Fast Retransmit (3 Duplicate ACKs)
children.details: Infer single packet loss early from 3 duplicate ACKs; retransmits without waiting for RTO timeout.

children.name: 6.4 TCP Tahoe vs Reno vs NewReno Disambiguation
children.details:
Evolution of TCP Congestion Control Algorithms

Algorithm Reaction to Timeout Reaction to 3 Duplicate ACKs
TCP Tahoe (1988) ssthresh = cwnd/2
cwnd = 1 MSS
Enter Slow Start		 Same as timeout:
ssthresh = cwnd/2
cwnd = 1 MSS
Enter Slow Start (Harsh penalty)
TCP Reno (1990) ssthresh = cwnd/2
cwnd = 1 MSS
Enter Slow Start		 Fast Recovery:
ssthresh = cwnd/2
cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS
Skips Slow Start! Stays in Congestion Avoidance.
TCP NewReno (1999) ssthresh = cwnd/2
cwnd = 1 MSS
Enter Slow Start		 Handles Multiple Drops: Remains in Fast Recovery upon receiving Partial ACKs, retransmitting subsequent lost packets without waiting for timeout.

children.name: Tahoe: Drops cwnd to 1 MSS on any loss
children.details: Always resets to cwnd=1 and slow starts, severely punishing throughput on isolated drops.

children.name: Reno: Fast Recovery (Halves cwnd)
children.details: On 3 dup ACKs, cuts cwnd to ssthresh and maintains data clocking in Fast Recovery.

children.name: NewReno: Partial ACKs in Fast Recovery
children.details: Tracks full and partial ACKs during Fast Recovery to repair multiple lost packets in one RTT.

children.name: 7. RTT Estimation & Timer Engineering
children.details:
TCP Round-Trip Time & Timer Mechanics

Accurate RTT calculation is vital. Setting RTO too short causes unnecessary duplicate transmissions; setting RTO too long causes slow recovery.

children.name: 7.1 Jacobson's Adaptive EWMA Algorithm
children.details:
Jacobson's RTT & Deviation Estimator (RFC 6298)

Calculates moving average and variance to dynamically adapt to network jitter:

  1. EstimatedRTT (EWMA): $$\text{EstimatedRTT} = (1 - \alpha) \times \text{EstimatedRTT} + \alpha \times \text{SampleRTT}$$ Recommended value: $\alpha = 0.125$ ($1/8$).
  2. DevRTT (Mean Absolute Deviation): $$\text{DevRTT} = (1 - \beta) \times \text{DevRTT} + \beta \times |\text{SampleRTT} - \text{EstimatedRTT}|$$ Recommended value: $\beta = 0.25$ ($1/4$).
  3. TimeoutInterval (RTO): $$\text{TimeoutInterval} = \text{EstimatedRTT} + 4 \times \text{DevRTT}$$

Safety Margin: The $4 \times \text{DevRTT}$ margin prevents spurious timeouts during temporary packet delay spikes.

children.name: EstimatedRTT (alpha = 0.125)
children.details: Exponentially Weighted Moving Average filters out transient RTT fluctuations.

children.name: DevRTT (beta = 0.25)
children.details: Tracks dispersion / jitter in round trip times.

children.name: RTO = EstimatedRTT + 4 * DevRTT
children.details: Dynamic safety margin; scales automatically with network variance.

children.name: 7.2 Karn's Algorithm (Retransmission Ambiguity)
children.details:
Disambiguation: The Retransmission Ambiguity Flaw (Slide 320 Diagram)

The Flaw: If a packet is retransmitted after timeout, and an ACK arrives:

  • Did the ACK acknowledge the 1st transmission (delayed) or the 2nd transmission (retransmitted)?
  • If sender assumes 1st: SampleRTT is huge and false!
  • If sender assumes 2nd: SampleRTT is artificially tiny!

Karn's Two Rules:

  1. Rule 1: Do NOT update EstimatedRTT or DevRTT using SampleRTT measured on retransmitted segments.
  2. Rule 2 (Exponential Backoff): Upon every retransmission timeout, double the RTO: $$RTO_{\text{new}} = 2 \times RTO_{\text{old}}$$ Once an ACK arrives for an un-retransmitted segment, normal Jacobson calculation resumes.

children.name: Retransmission Ambiguity Flaw
children.details: Inability to determine if an ACK corresponds to the original or retransmitted segment.

children.name: Karn's Solution: Discard Sample & Double RTO
children.details: Never measure SampleRTT on retransmissions; back off timer exponentially (2x RTO) on timeout.

children.name: 7.3 The 4 Essential TCP Timers
children.details:
The 4 Essential TCP Timers & Operating Scenarios

  • 1. Retransmission Timer (RTO): Detects lost segments. Backs off exponentially on repeated loss.
  • 2. Persistence Timer: Prevents zero-window deadlock when receiver ACK update is lost. Sends 1-byte probes.
  • 3. Keepalive Timer: Detects dead clients in established connections. Default: 2 hours idle -> 10 probes at 75s intervals -> reset connection if no reply.
  • 4. TIME_WAIT Timer: Runs for $2 \times \text{MSL}$ (60–120s) after active close to drain old packets and guarantee final ACK reception.

children.name: Retransmission Timer (RTO)
children.details: Recovers from lost segments. Backs off exponentially upon retransmissions.

children.name: Persistence Timer
children.details: Probes zero-window condition to break deadlocks.

children.name: Keepalive Timer (2 Hours)
children.details: Cleans up orphaned connections where client crashed without sending FIN.

children.name: TIME_WAIT Timer (2MSL)
children.details: Quarantines socket pair for 2MSL to prevent ghost packet collisions.

children.name: 8. User Datagram Protocol (UDP) & Connectionless Transport
children.details:
UDP Architecture & Minimal Transport Abstraction (RFC 768)

UDP provides bare-bones, connectionless multiplexing and integrity check over IP.

children.name: 8.1 TCP vs UDP Deep Disambiguation
children.details:
Deep Architectural Disambiguation: TCP vs UDP

Property TCP UDP
Connection State Connection-oriented (3-way handshake, state maintained in TCB). Connectionless (zero setup latency, stateless).
Reliability Reliable, in-order byte stream. Retransmits missing bytes. Unreliable datagrams. Packets may be lost, duplicated, or reordered.
Header Overhead 20 – 60 Bytes 8 Bytes fixed
Congestion Control Throttles transmission rate during network congestion. No throttling. Sends at application rate (ideal for real-time audio/video and DNS).

children.name: Stateless vs Stateful TCB
children.details: UDP holds no connection context; TCP allocates ~10-20KB buffers and control blocks per socket.

children.name: Unregulated Sending Rate
children.details: UDP transmits as fast as the application generates data, without AIMD rate reduction.

children.name: 8.2 UDP 8-Byte Header & Checksum Architecture
children.details:
UDP Header Fields & 1's Complement Checksum

  • 8-Byte Header:
    1. Source Port (16 bits) - Optional, 0 if unused.
    2. Destination Port (16 bits) - Mandatory for demux.
    3. Length (16 bits) - Total bytes of UDP header + data (minimum 8).
    4. Checksum (16 bits) - Error detection over pseudo-header + header + data.
  • Pseudo-Header Inclusion: Checksum includes 12 bytes from IP header (Source IP, Dest IP, 0x00, Protocol 17, UDP Length). Prevents misrouted packets from being accepted by wrong host!

children.name: 8-Byte Header Layout
children.details: Source Port (2B), Destination Port (2B), Length (2B), Checksum (2B).

children.name: Pseudo-Header & 1's Complement Sum
children.details: Calculates checksum over IP endpoints to catch misrouted packets.

children.name: 9. Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL) & Cryptography
children.details:
Transport Layer Security Architecture

TLS secures transport layer communication by providing Confidentiality (Symmetric Encryption), Integrity (HMAC), and Endpoint Authentication (X.509 Certificates / Asymmetric Key Cryptography).

children.name: 9.1 The 4-Phase TLS Handshake (Slide 359 Diagram)
children.details:
The 4-Phase TLS Handshake Progression

  1. Phase 1: Establish Security Capabilities:
    • ClientHello: Supported cipher suites, client random ($R_c$), TLS version.
    • ServerHello: Chosen cipher suite, server random ($R_s$), Session ID.
  2. Phase 2: Server Authentication & Key Exchange:
    • Certificate: Server's X.509 public key certificate signed by CA.
    • ServerKeyExchange: Diffie-Hellman parameters (if ephemeral DH used).
    • ServerHelloDone: Signals end of server negotiation messages.
  3. Phase 3: Client Authentication & Key Exchange:
    • ClientKeyExchange: Client sends Pre-Master Secret (PMS) encrypted with Server's RSA public key (or Client DH share).
  4. Phase 4: Cipher Activation & Finish:
    • ChangeCipherSpec: Both sides activate negotiated cryptographic algorithms.
    • Finished: First encrypted message containing HMAC over all prior handshake messages to prevent tampering / downgrade attacks.

children.name: Phase 1: Security Capabilities
children.details: ClientHello & ServerHello negotiate cipher suite and exchange random nonces Rc, Rs.

children.name: Phase 2: Server Auth & Key Exchange
children.details: Server presents X.509 certificate and optional Diffie-Hellman parameters.

children.name: Phase 3: Client Key Exchange
children.details: Client generates and transmits 48-byte Pre-Master Secret encrypted under server's public key.

children.name: Phase 4: Finished & Cipher Activation
children.details: ChangeCipherSpec activates encryption; Finished validates handshake integrity via HMAC.

children.name: 9.2 Key Derivation Hierarchy
children.details:
Master Secret & 4 Session Keys Derivation

Both client and server independently compute the 48-byte Master Secret using the Pseudo-Random Function (PRF):

$$\text{Master Secret} = \text{PRF}(\text{Pre-Master Secret}, \text{"master secret"}, R_c + R_s)$$

The Master Secret is expanded into a key block sliced into 4 distinct operational keys:

  1. Client Write MAC Key: Client integrity generation; Server integrity verification.
  2. Server Write MAC Key: Server integrity generation; Client integrity verification.
  3. Client Write Encryption Key: Client data encryption; Server decryption.
  4. Server Write Encryption Key: Server data encryption; Client decryption.

children.name: Pre-Master Secret -> 48-Byte Master Secret
children.details: Calculated via PRF over Pre-Master Secret and random nonces Rc, Rs.

children.name: 4 Sliced Operational Keys
children.details: Client/Server Write MAC keys (integrity) and Client/Server Write Encryption keys (confidentiality).

children.name: 9.3 TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3 Disambiguation (Slide 366 Diagram)
children.details:
Disambiguation: TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3 Architecture

Metric TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)
Handshake Latency 2 RTT (after TCP handshake) 1 RTT (0-RTT with PSK resumption!)
Key Exchange Mechanism RSA static key transport allowed. Server communicates key in Phase 2. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman only (DHE/ECDHE). Client sends key share speculatively in ClientHello.
Forward Secrecy Optional (compromised RSA private key decrypts past recorded traffic). Mandatory Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS).
Permitted Cipher Suites 30+ legacy suites including RC4, 3DES, CBC-mode ciphers. Only 5 AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Stripped insecure ciphers.

children.name: 1-RTT Handshake & 0-RTT Resumption
children.details: Client sends key shares speculatively in ClientHello, cutting handshake latency by half.

children.name: Mandatory Forward Secrecy (PFS)
children.details: Bans static RSA key exchange; ephemeral Diffie-Hellman guarantees past sessions cannot be decrypted.

children.name: AEAD Only Ciphers
children.details: Bans vulnerable CBC, RC4, and 3DES modes; mandates authenticated encryption.

children.name: 10. The Master Disambiguation Matrix
children.details:
The Master Networking Disambiguation Matrix

Direct head-to-head comparisons resolving frequently confused networking mechanisms, protocols, and algorithmic boundaries.

children.name: 10.1 Flow Control vs Congestion Control
children.details:
Disambiguation 1: Flow Control vs Congestion Control

Flow Control: Protects the receiver host buffer. Advertised in TCP header as rwnd.

Congestion Control: Protects network routers from queue collapse. Maintained locally as cwnd.

Governing Equation: Effective Window $W = \min(\text{rwnd}, \text{cwnd})$.

children.name: 10.2 Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat
children.details:
Disambiguation 2: Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat

  • GBN: Cumulative ACK, single timer for oldest packet, discards out-of-order packets, retransmits entire window $N$. Window constraint $N \le 2^k - 1$.
  • SR: Individual ACKs, independent timer per unacked packet, buffers out-of-order packets, retransmits only lost packets. Window constraint $N \le 2^{k-1}$.

children.name: 10.3 TCP vs UDP
children.details:
Disambiguation 3: TCP vs UDP

  • TCP: Connection-oriented, 4-tuple demux, reliable byte stream, flow & congestion control, 20-60B header.
  • UDP: Connectionless, 2-tuple demux, unreliable datagrams, application-driven rate, 8B fixed header.

children.name: 10.4 TCP Tahoe vs TCP Reno vs TCP NewReno
children.details:
Disambiguation 4: Tahoe vs Reno vs NewReno

  • Tahoe (1988): On any loss (timeout or 3 dup ACKs) -> ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1, enters Slow Start.
  • Reno (1990): On 3 dup ACKs -> Fast Recovery: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh + 3, skips Slow Start.
  • NewReno (1999): Resolves Reno flaw on multiple packet losses using Partial ACKs to keep retransmitting without timing out.

children.name: 10.5 HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
children.details:
Disambiguation 5: Web Protocol Evolution & HOL Blocking

  • HTTP/1.1: Persistent TCP; suffers from Application-level Head-of-Line blocking.
  • HTTP/2: Multiplexed binary streams over 1 TCP connection; suffers from TCP-level Head-of-Line blocking.
  • HTTP/3: Independent streams over QUIC/UDP; completely eliminates Head-of-Line blocking.

children.name: 10.6 Nagle's Algorithm vs Clark's Solution
children.details:
Disambiguation 6: Silly Window Syndrome Solutions

  • Nagle's Algorithm (Sender): Buffer small outgoing packets until full MSS is formed or until previous ACK returns.
  • Clark's Solution (Receiver): Do not advertise window until space is at least $\min(\text{MSS}, \text{Buffer}/2)$.

children.name: 10.7 Karn's Algorithm (Retransmission Ambiguity)
children.details:
Disambiguation 7: The Retransmission Ambiguity Flaw

  • The Flaw: ACKs for retransmitted packets cannot be correlated with the 1st or 2nd transmission, corrupting RTT estimates.
  • Karn's Solution: Never calculate SampleRTT on retransmissions; exponentially double RTO ($RTO_{\text{new}} = 2 \times RTO_{\text{old}}$) upon timeout.

children.name: 10.8 TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3
children.details:
Disambiguation 8: TLS Handshake Latency & Cipher Hardening

  • TLS 1.2: 2 RTT handshake latency; permits legacy vulnerable ciphers (RC4, DES, CBC).
  • TLS 1.3: 1 RTT handshake latency (with 0-RTT resumption); client sends key share speculatively in ClientHello; mandates AEAD ciphers.
